title: The Fox Who Borrowed Tomorrow
summary: When a repair takes longer than he promised, Rin borrows seven minutes from the valley clock. The debt costs his friend Tala her last breakfast with her father before winter. Now a red sail is disappearing around the bend, and Tala has a shortcut in mind.
style: Sumi ink and watercolor on warm paper, with moss green, vermilion and brass.
coverAlt: Rin, a red fox in a moss-green vest, holds a brass clock wheel. Tala, a brown river otter in an indigo apron, cradles a blue flowered tea tin. Behind them a red-sailed ferry crosses a misty canal below a bell and a windmill.

pages.alt: An autumn canal runs past a cottage full of clocks. Beneath the lock bell, Rin the fox steadies a delicate wooden cricket on his workbench with both black paws.
pages.transcript:
At Willow Lock the valley set its kettles, its clocks and its ferries by Rin’s bell.

Tala had trusted him with her father’s clockwork cricket. The right wing sang like rain. The left went click.

pages.alt: Tala, a brown otter in a blue apron, appears at Rin’s door with her flowered tea tin. Later they dangle their feet above the water beside three clay cups and a red-sailed ferry.
pages.transcript:
“Forget the cricket if you have to,” Tala said. “Promise you’ll ring seven minutes early tomorrow.”

“Dad sails at six. Tea takes two minutes. His terrible joke takes three. The last two are mine.”

pages.alt: By lantern and moonlight, Rin fits a carved crescent wing onto the cricket. He opens the canal clock and finds an extra winding handle behind its brass gears.
pages.transcript:
By midnight the new wing still scraped. Rin could just see Tala’s face if he handed it back singing.

Behind the clock was a crank with seven teeth. Each tooth lent the keeper one minute. The first bell of tomorrow collected the debt.

pages.alt: Rin’s black paw turns a brass key while small amber lights escape the clock. Beyond his lit workbench, leaves and beads of water hang in the moonlight.
pages.transcript:
One minute for the glue. Two for the spring. Then three, four, five, six. The seventh came away almost by itself.

Outside, a raindrop waited at the eaves. At his bench Rin wound the cricket. Both wings opened. It sang.

pages.alt: A heron pours hot water beside a startled baker. Tala runs down the wet steps carrying her tin and tea tray as a loose mooring rope flicks through the air.
pages.transcript:
At dawn a kettle jumped from cold to boiling. A baker blinked. Seven minutes had gone by inside the blink.

Tala heard six bells when she’d been waiting for the early one. She ran with the tea still dry.

pages.alt: Rin holds the cricket while Tala looks after a very small red sail. Her paw closes the blue tea tin beside three empty cups and the little toy.
pages.transcript:
Only the red point of her father’s sail showed beyond the bend. Rin wound the cricket. It sang to an empty wharf.

“You said you’d ring. He won’t be back till the thaw.” Tala shut the tin. “Where did my seven minutes go, Rin?”

pages.alt: Rin points to empty spaces in a brass wheel while Tala watches from the door. Inside, she moves a wooden stool and faces him with one paw open.
pages.transcript:
“Here.” Rin showed her the wheel. “I spent them on the cricket. I knew where they came from.”

“I like Dad’s terrible joke,” Tala said. “I like how he laughs before he gets to the end. Did you think to ask?”

pages.alt: On the towpath the fox walks ahead with a gap between them. Tala kneels on the mossy stone and lowers her twine and plumb bob into circling water.
pages.transcript:
Rin reached for the crank. Tala shook her head. “I’ve lost my morning. Leave everybody else’s alone.”

She dipped a line in the current. “He has to wait at the lower lock. Come with me. Bring your paws.”

pages.alt: Tala marks the canal’s two channels in wet mud. On the narrow mossy shortcut she catches Rin by the paw as he loses his footing.
pages.transcript:
Tala scratched two channels in the mud. The ferry needed deep water. Two friends on foot could take the old mill cut.

The moss slid from under Rin. Tala caught his wrist. “That’s one paw,” she said. “I’ll need the other in a minute.”

pages.alt: At the lower lock a fallen wooden peg blocks the great wheel with the red-sailed ferry approaching. Tala measures the broken linkage with twine as Rin examines it.
pages.transcript:
They reached the lower lock ahead of the ferry. A peg had split inside the wheel. The gates stayed shut.

Tala looped twine round the socket. “Straight brass, this thick.” Rin laid the cricket across the loop. Its axle fitted exactly.

pages.alt: Rin shows Tala the wooden cricket up close. Its brass axle and carved wings come apart as they prepare a repair for the gate.
pages.transcript:
“That’s his present,” Tala said. “I know,” said Rin. “You asked for my paws. Tell me where to put them.”

He eased the pin through both wings. This time he let the thing he’d made come apart.

pages.alt: With Rin bracing the wheel, Tala hammers the cricket’s axle into the linkage. Water carries the red-sailed ferry into the opened lock.
pages.transcript:
“Brace the wheel. Mind your tail.” Rin held. On the third tap Tala drove the pin home.

The ferry rose to the stone step. A grey-whiskered otter looked up. “Anyone put the kettle on?”

pages.alt: Tala shares her blue tea tin and cups with her father, a grey-whiskered otter in an ochre cap. Rin keeps hold of the line while the two otters laugh.
pages.transcript:
Rin took the line. Tala set down the cups. Her father filled hers first, just as he did at home.

“Two banks this river’s got,” Dad said. He started laughing. “Not a penny between them!” Tala laughed into her cup.

pages.alt: The red sail passes down the tree-lined canal as Tala waves. Back at the clock room, Rin reaches up to hang the brass key beside his tools.
pages.transcript:
They had four minutes. Tala used the last one to sit shoulder to shoulder with her father, saying nothing at all.

Back home Rin hung up the crank key. “Next time I’m late, I’ll tell you I’m late.” Tala nodded. “I can work with late.”

pages.alt: Rin and Tala drink tea together on a coil of rope beside the canal. A little green cricket lands on the wooden wings beside their empty cups.
pages.transcript:
Next morning they met before the bell. Tala poured. Rin drank his tea while it was hot.

Something chirruped. On two wooden wings stood a perfectly ordinary cricket, keeping its own time.
